rows.q: Mirae Asset Large Cap 5 year CAGR
rows.raw: CAGR, or compound annual growth rate, tells you the smooth, average speed at which an investment has grown each year over a set period, such as five years. Think of it as the steady pace you’d need to maintain every year to turn the starting amount into the current value, ignoring the ups and downs that happened along the way. When you look at this figure, a higher number simply means the investment has moved faster on average, while a lower number indicates a slower pace of growth. It’s a handy way to compare how quickly different investments have progressed over the same length of time.

rows.q: How much has ICICI Prudential Value Fund returned in 2 years?
rows.raw: Total return tells you the overall change in the value of an investment over a chosen time span, combining both the movement in its market price and any income it has generated, such as dividends. When you look at this figure, a higher number means the investment has grown more, while a lower number indicates less growth or a decline. It lets you see the complete picture of how the investment performed, rather than just the price alone, making it easier to compare results across different periods or options.

rows.q: max drawdown of nippon india small cap over 5 years
rows.raw: Maximum drawdown tells you how much the value of an investment fell from its highest point to its lowest point over a given time span. Think of it as the deepest dip you would have experienced if you had been holding the investment throughout that period. It’s a way to gauge the worst‑case loss you might have faced, helping you understand how volatile or risky the investment can be during market downturns. When you see the figure, picture the peak value and then the lowest trough that followed; the difference between them is the maximum drawdown. This gives a simple snapshot of the investment’s biggest historical setback.

rows.q: Volatility of HDFC Balanced Advantage over 3 years
rows.raw: Annualised volatility is a way of describing how much the value of an investment tends to move up and down over the course of a year. Think of it as the size of the roller‑coaster ride: a higher number means the price swings more wildly, while a lower number indicates a smoother, steadier ride. When you look at this figure, simply compare it with other numbers you see—whichever is higher points to bigger fluctuations, and whichever is lower points to more calm, predictable changes. This helps you get a feel for how “bouncy” the investment can be.

rows.q: SIP of 3000 rupees every month on the 10th in Parag Parikh Flexi Cap for 4 years: what XIRR?
rows.raw: The XIRR for a systematic investment plan shows the annual growth rate you’ve earned, taking into account each monthly contribution and the exact dates they were made. It works like a speedometer for your investment, converting all the cash‑in and cash‑out moments into a single yearly figure that reflects how fast the money has been compounding. When you look at the number, a larger value indicates that the investment has been growing more quickly over the period, while a smaller value points to slower growth. This helps you compare the performance of different plans or time spans without worrying about the exact timing of each payment.

rows.q: XIRR if I invested Rs 1,500 monthly in SBI Contra for 6 years
rows.raw: SIP XIRR is a way to show the average yearly growth you get when you put money in regularly, such as a fixed amount each month, over a period of time. It works by looking at every cash flow – when you add money and when you get it back – and calculates a single rate that would make the total of those flows equal to the final amount. The result is expressed as a percent and lets you compare how fast your investment has been growing, regardless of the exact dates of each contribution. A higher number simply indicates a faster pace of growth compared with a lower one.
